Part 5: HCF Euclid s Algorithm
Challenge (skip ahead if you can): Write using Euclid s method reuse your function from Part 4 to get the remainder. Got it? Skip to Part 6 .

The HCF (Highest Common Factor) of two numbers is the largest number that divides both of them evenly. It s also called the GCD (Greatest Common Divisor). Example: the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. The highest factor they share is 6 .

fragments.text: Nobody taught you these you derived them yourself . Every recursive algorithm you meet from here on searching, sorting, tree traversal leans on exactly this idea: trust that a smaller call works, and build the bigger answer on top of it.

slide_text: Reflection what did you just build? Every recursive function has a base case and a recursive case. What goes wrong if either is missing or the recursive case never gets closer to the base case? In Part 2, handling negative showed a pattern: convert the hard case into one you already solved. Where else did you use this pattern? In Part 5, you reused from Part 4 instead of reimplementing . Why is reusing better? Hanoi and Fibonacci both make two recursive calls per step. What s different about how their total work grows? What is memoization, and what problem does it solve?
